content:
A little thought experiment...

Imagine you are offered a huge pack of money for a sorry-free proof of FLT (Fermat's Last Theorem) in Lean 4.29.0 (and, of course, you cannot mess with the statement of FLT). It doesn't matter how you obtain the proof — if you submit a sorry-free proof of FLT in Lean 4.29.0, you will get the money.

Do you expect it to be cheaper to go ahead and actually prove it, or to find a kernel bug and prove False in order to obtain a sorry-free proof of FLT? Of course, we don't know whether it is possible. Nevertheless, I would like to know your gut feeling about which of the ways to write a sorry-free proof of FLT in Lean 4.29.0 would be cheaper.

Kevin has received about 1 million pound for his Formalising Fermat grant. I think you will be able to find a bug in the default kernel for 1 million pound. Whether you will find one that passes both nanoda and the default kernel and potentially upcoming kernels is an entirely different question though.

I didn't want to bring up the topic of @Kevin Buzzard having a grant for FLT because it isn't like "if he doesn't have a sorry-free proof at the end of the grant period, he will have to return the money". This is a thought experiment, unrelated to grant agencies.

Thanks for the point that it would be a very different challenge to have to pass both the default kernel and nanoda!
I guess it matters whom you ask. Mathematicians may find it easer to actually prove it, compiler and theorem prover experts will find it easier to find a kernel bug?
